entries.title: Armed Man Arrested at Trump’s LA Golf Course Ahead of the President’s Visit
entries.summary: Deputies found a loaded pistol with a 16-round magazine containing hollow-point ammunition on the man, the sheriff’s office said.
entries.content:
A heavily armed man was arrested at President Donald Trump’s golf course in Los Angeles days before his Tuesday fundraiser there, authorities said.

Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department deputies detained Jeanine John Taele, 38, on Sunday after he was seen taking photos and “appearing to monitor security-planning activities” at the Trump National Golf Course in Rancho Palos Verdes, the sheriff’s office said.

Taele was arrested on suspicion of carrying a concealed firearm and possessing prohibited ammunition after the deputies found a 16-round magazine containing hollow-point ammunition tucked into his pants, along with a loaded pistol and additional ammunition in his car, according to a statement from the sheriff’s office.

Deputies later searched his residence and found an illegally modified AR-style rifle, body armor, more high-capacity magazines and notebooks consisting of “concerning statements.” The deputies also discovered that Taele was under investigation for robbery by the El Segundo Police Department, the sheriff’s office said.

Trump was aboard Air Force One on his way to speak at a Republican National Committee fundraiser at the golf course when authorities first announced the arrest Tuesday afternoon.

The FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force and the Secret Service are investigating, but authorities have determined there is “no credible threat,” the sheriff’s office said. The Secret Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: Missouri Elections Official Blocks Petition Challenging GOP-Friendly Redistricting Map
entries.summary: Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said the petition had the requisite number of signatures but was still “unconstitutional.”
entries.content:
Missouri’s top elections official squashed a challenge to Republicans’ new congressional map that could net them one more U.S. House seat, waiting until the last possible day to block a petition that would have triggered a statewide vote on the gerrymander.

Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, on Tuesday rejected petitioners’ attempt to put the map on the ballot in November ahead of the deadline to decide whether the petition could advance, saying the challenge itself was “unconstitutional.”

“At issue is not the number of signatures turned into the challenge, the new congressional map, but the fact that the referendum itself is null and void by virtue of the fact that it is unconstitutional,” Hoskins said at a Tuesday press conference. “Therefore, House Bill 1, the Missouri First map, continues to be the law of the land.”

Hoskins also said that Gov. Mike Kehoe and Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway agreed with his choice. At the press conference, Hoskins said he was “confident in the stance” he's taken, and that the government is “prepared to go to court.”

That chance will come soon: People Not Politicians Missouri, the group that led the original petition, confirmed in a statement Tuesday evening that it plans to announce details regarding future litigation tomorrow.

The Missouri General Assembly pushed through a new map targeting Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s heavily Democratic district, becoming one of the first states that moved to redistrict after President Donald Trump pushed state lawmakers to redraw their congressional maps to more heavily favor Republicans.

Signed into law by Kehoe last September, the map carves Missouri’s largest city, Kansas City, into three congressional districts.

Shortly after the assembly pushed the new lines through last fall, People Not Politicians Missouri gathered over 300,000 signatures to force a referendum. In Missouri, a petition with enough signatures triggers a veto referendum, or a statewide vote on the law in question.

The group filed the signatures in December. Hoskins had until 5 p.m. Tuesday to decide on the legality of the petition — the same day as Missouri’s primary elections.

Hoskins was widely expected to not certify the signatures, previously saying that any signatures gathered before the campaign was approved by his office constituted “a misdemeanor election offense,” a claim his office later clarified and corrected.

“Secretary of State Hoskins is making a last desperate attempt to silence the people’s voice in Missouri,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, wrote in a statement. “We’ve fought back against politicians for the last year, and we won’t stop now. There are more than enough signatures, verified by election authorities, to qualify the referendum.”

entries.title: HHS Awards Small Texas Firm With $150M Contract to Represent Unaccompanied Children
entries.summary: The Burke Law Group could now be tasked with representing over 20,000 children in immigration proceedings.
entries.content:
The Department of Health and Human Services revealed plans to award a multimillion-dollar contract to a small Texas law firm, tasking it with representing thousands of immigrant children as they face immigration court proceedings.

HHS’s refugee resettlement division — charged with overseeing unaccompanied undocumented children — had a contract with the Acacia Center for Justice that was not renewed after expiring last Friday. The federal government had a fraught relationship with Acacia, including attempting to terminate its legal contract last March and withholding funding for months. Nonprofits have sued to get the agency to pay invoices dating back to December totaling roughly $65 million, the groups announced last week.

On Thursday, Acacia said its legal teams had defended more than 20,000 children despite not being paid. In a Tuesday statement before the new contract was published, the organization said it was “adamant” whoever took over the contract must have “deep experience” with the country’s immigration system.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement quietly awarded the new contract — worth up to $150 million per year — to the Burke Law Group, a boutique law firm headquartered in Houston. No one at the organization specializes in immigration law, according to staff biographies on the website, though the site lists “immigration and asylum” as one of two-dozen practice areas on a separate page.

The firm would “provide legal orientation, legal consultation and attorney-of-record representation services” for unaccompanied immigrant children while under Office of Refugee Resettlement care, the agreement reads, and help connect them with legal resources after being discharged. The federal government has been required to help facilitate legal counsel for unaccompanied children in Office of Refugee Resettlement custody since 2008.

Founder and managing partner Marcella Burke worked in President Donald Trump’s first administration, serving as deputy general counsel in the Environmental Protection Agency before moving to the Department of the Interior, according to her LinkedIn profile. She is also a board member for the Federalist Society Houston Lawyers Chapter, according to a release noting her appointment by Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to the Texas School Land Board.

“The purpose of this proposed award is to provide legal orientation, legal consultation, and attorney-of-record representation services for eligible unaccompanied children (UACs) during immigration proceedings,” the notice, which is set to be officially published on the Federal Register on Thursday, read.

The contract is set to go into effect on Aug. 15 and last one year.

entries.title: Chuck Edwards Ends His Reelection Following Harassment Allegations
entries.summary: The House Ethics Committee had recommended the North Carolina Republican be censured.
entries.content:
Rep. Chuck Edwards suspended his campaign for reelection early Wednesday morning following a House Ethics report that cited alleged inappropriate behavior toward two women staffers.

“After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign,” he posted on X. “I will complete my current term. Serving Western North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support. God bless WNC and America.”

The Ethics committee recommended on Monday that the North Carolina Republican be censured and found “substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces,” according to a committee press release.

Edwards was running for reelection in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, one of two competitive districts in the state crucial to both parties’ path to a majority in Congress.

Pressure had been building among Republicans to force him out.

House Republicans were privately trying to convince Edwards to abandon his reelection bid in light of the House Ethics committee’s report, CNN reported on Tuesday. A source on Capitol Hill told The News & Observer that Sen. Ted Budd (R-North Carolina) asked Edwards to drop out of the race.

A spokesperson for Budd told NOTUS on Tuesday that while the senator doesn’t disclose his private conversations, he “finds the House Ethics report deeply concerning.” The spokesperson added that Budd "believes Rep. Edwards faces a significant uphill battle in his reelection bid,” pointing to Edwards’ trailing poll numbers and that his opponent is vastly outraising Edwards.

Since Edwards withdrew from the race before military and overseas absentee ballots were distributed on Sept. 4, state law says the North Carolina 11th District GOP Executive Committee, which includes the district party’s officers as well as other members, can choose Edwards’ replacement on the ballot.

The House Ethics Committee found that Edwards gave the two women staffers “lavish gifts,” including expensive jewelry, designer purses, vacations, guns, and dinners.

The report also pointed to instances when Edwards paid for spa trips, talked to staffers about going to D.C. strip clubs, and told one of the staffers not to let his scheduler know about a dinner the two had planned.

The committee did not find evidence that Edwards “engaged in sexual activity with or explicitly propositioned any individual under his employ.” The report said that Edwards was aware that his “excessive attention toward the young women had led to rumors and innuendo in the office” and “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate.”  

Even before news broke about him being the subject of a House Ethics investigation in May, Edwards faced a competitive challenge from Democrat Jamie Ager, a farmer backed by the centrist group Blue Dog Democrats who comes from a family of North Carolina politicians.

Ager is one of several Democrats running in red districts that have the backing of House Democrats’ campaign arm through its Red to Blue program. The Cook Political Report changed the district’s rating from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican” in June.

The state’s other competitive seat is North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, currently held by Democrat Rep. Don Davis.

entries.title: The Key Economic Warning Sign That Could Upend the Midterms
entries.summary: Turbulence in the bond market is near levels where “things start to break,” economists warn.
entries.content:
When President Donald Trump suddenly backed off his massive “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025, he acknowledged his reversal had been driven by one factor in particular: “I was watching the bond market. The bond market is very tricky … People were getting a little queasy.”

Over the past week, the bond market has looked more than a little queasy. The deterioration of arguably the most critical financial asset in the world now risks rippling through the broader U.S. economy in dangerous and unpredictable ways — and possibly right before the 2026 midterm elections.

On Friday, the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond reached a nearly two-decade high of 5.3%, and has only partly come back down since then. The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond spiked above 4.7% — the highest level since the beginning of the Trump administration. It recovered on Monday and Tuesday, but remains near recent highs.

“Five percent is really when things start to break,” said Joseph Brusuelas, principal and chief economist for RSM US LLP, of the 10-year Treasury bond yield. “You don’t know where it’s going to be. But if rates surge, it’s going to cause some problems in those institutions. And then who knows what can go wrong next.”

Economists and Wall Street analysts generally agree that the risks to small- and medium-sized banks grow substantially if 30-year Treasury bond yields rise above 6% and 10-year Treasury bond yields rise above 5%. They say both numbers are worryingly within reach.

The last sustained period of high interest rates led to the failure of Silicon Valley Bank, precipitating a bailout from the Biden administration to prevent a broader financial contagion from dragging down the U.S. economy.

The $40 trillion in outstanding debt issued by the federal government is a pillar of the global economy. The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond is the benchmark for mortgage rates, housing loans, credit card payments and a host of other critical functions, in addition to serving as the reserves for countries around the world. Already high borrowing costs have made it more expensive to take out a mortgage, buy a car or start a business, and have also driven up the costs to taxpayers of financing the debt.

Trump's been feeling the squeeze: his approval rating on the economy dropped from 38% to 30% from March to April, according to an Associated Press poll. Democrats’ approval ratings generally are also abysmal, but they should benefit if voters take out their anger over the economy on the president — especially if new problems emerge in the next three months.

On Wednesday morning, the Treasury Department will announce plans for later Treasury auctions to borrow an additional $739 billion to fulfill government payments between July and September. This will be a key gauge of investors’ appetite for buying more U.S. debt despite the recent concerns. Any shortage of investor appetite could trigger another sharp rise in bond yields.

“Between now and the midterms, probably the biggest risks are some kind of failed Treasury auction,” said Adam Posen, president of the Peterson Institute for International Economics, a centrist think tank. “It’s like so many other things where people adapt and reset expectations because the world didn’t end last time, so I won’t overreact this time. That’s only true until it isn’t.”

Trump’s declared “Liberation Day” tariffs triggered a financial market panic in which investors dumped billions in U.S. treasuries. Faced with the broad economic fallout of the bond market crisis, Trump suspended most of his import duties at the last moment. Markets recovered with relative ease.

The spike this time was less sudden and has gotten less attention. But it may also be harder to resolve.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh last week fueled doubts about the central bank’s willingness to hike interest rates to fight inflation. This drove investors out of long-term bonds, because out-of-control inflation reduces the value of the dollar over time. Warsh has been under pressure from Trump not to raise interest rates because they slow down economic growth.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday expressed optimism that prices are generally heading in the right direction, which would put less pressure on Warsh to raise interest rates. But other economists have been skeptical, noting that inflation remains well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.

“What gives me the confidence is that the underlying numbers — they are very tame,” Bessent said on CNBC. “I think we're going to continue to see that.”

Even if Warsh can preserve the central bank’s inflation-fighting credibility, there may be other threats to the bond market that could prove harder to untangle than calling off the “Liberation Day” tariffs.

Japan is the second-largest holder of U.S. treasuries in the world, with $1.1 trillion in holdings. But Japan has faced a severe currency crisis of its own, and moved to sell treasuries to prop up the value of the yen, in turn putting further pressure on U.S. bonds. Bessent stepped in this week to prop up the yen, and while that effort has looked successful thus far it may prove a temporary salve.

An escalation in hostilities with Iran could also lead to another surge in bond yields. Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWD Bonds, said “the big swings” in oil prices tied to the resumption of fighting have been perhaps an even greater cause of volatility, as investors rush to beat the market. Bonds calmed after Trump's latest comments over the weekend that a deal with Iran was within reach, but then the president has also threatened the country with "decapitation" if it did not accept an agreement.

Even without the war or spillover from Japan, analysts say high yields will persist as long as the federal government continues to run annual deficits that are close to 6% of the national economy. While large deficits are unlikely to cause a market crisis, particularly in the short term, the fiscal imbalance still drives higher rates that raise borrowing costs for the government and therefore U.S. consumers.

“My view of the most likely scenario is that we have no acute crisis, but rates stay high in a way that is still a really big problem — the cost of homeownership continues to be a disaster, and consumers face high interest rates,” said Tobin Marcus, the head of U.S. policy and research at Wolfe Research and a former Biden economic official. “It’s a little hard to tell a story about a major catalyst where something big breaks, but it’s definitely possible.”

The odds of a deal to lower the deficit are vanishingly small, and that means the pressure will likely fall primarily on the Federal Reserve not to reprise last week’s disaster. If it cannot do so between now and November, the political impact may be felt sooner rather than later.

“If the concerns with the Fed grow, what we see with interest rates will just keep going higher,” said Claudia Sahm, a former economist with the central bank. “And regular people will notice that.”

entries.title: Freedom 250 Sponsors Failed to Disclose Donations — A Potential Lobbying Law Violation
entries.summary: Corporate giants such as Lockheed Martin, ExxonMobil and United Health Group could run afoul of the Lobbying Disclosure Act.
entries.content:
The Great American State Fair was covered in the logos of dozens of corporate lobbying giants.

But most of the event sponsors — including defense contractors Lockheed Martin, GE Aerospace and Northrop Grumman — did not disclose payments to the President Donald Trump-supported event organizer Freedom 250, in potential violation of federal lobbying law, according to a NOTUS review of federal lobbyist contribution reports due to Congress by last Friday.

The Great American State Fair was also “presented by” corporate giants including ExxonMobil, SAP, Exiger, Mosaic and ScottsMiracle-Gro, according to billboards NOTUS photographed around the fair grounds last month. They’re among the almost two-dozen companies, including Palantir, Oracle, UnitedHealth Group and John Deere, listed as “sponsors” on the Freedom 250 website.
LockheedMartin.State.Fair (4722x2656, AR: 1.78)Only three Freedom 250 corporate sponsors — Chevron, United Airlines and RTX — disclosed financial contributions to the organization as required by the federal Lobbying Disclosure Act. Ethics experts told NOTUS that the other companies should, too.

Under the Lobbying Disclosure Act, any entity that lobbies the federal government must file semiannual reports with Congress detailing honorary expenses, event cost payments and donations to political campaigns, presidential inaugurations, presidential libraries and other entities established or controlled by public officials.

The law “is certainly not airtight, and certain entities have found ways to try to exploit this law,” Aaron Scherb, a longtime ethics and democracy advocate, told NOTUS.

“Nonetheless, it requires full disclosure of political spending when companies are trying to curry favor with an administration and elected officials,” Scherb added. “So, companies contributing to Freedom 250 should absolutely be required to disclose their political spending.”

Freedom 250 was established by Task Force 250, which Trump created via executive order.

Trump himself is the chair of Freedom 250. The limited liability corporation is housed within the National Park Foundation, the nonprofit charity arm of the National Park Service, to which companies have previously disclosed donations.

“When it comes to other nonprofits, the question is always whether it was created and controlled by Trump,” Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist at the left-leaning nonprofit watchdog Public Citizen, told NOTUS. “But there is little question about Freedom 250.”

The offices of the clerk of the House and secretary of the Senate, which are tasked with processing lobbying disclosures and questioning lobbyists who fail to comply with reporting requirements, did not respond to requests for comment on obligations to disclose contributions to Freedom 250. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, which is tasked with enforcing compliance, also did not respond to questions.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Freedom 250 had raised $50 million from a variety of corporate interests. But the vast majority of these reported contributions — including $2 million from TikTok and $1 million each from Oracle and ExxonMobil — were not separately disclosed in certified federal disclosures, as required by the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

As of Tuesday evening, only three companies that both lobby the federal government and contributed money to Freedom 250 disclosed how much they gave to the Trump-backed organization.

Oil company Chevron, a presenting sponsor of the Great American State Fair, shelled out $5 million in May, according to federal records first reported by Politico and Sludge.

United Airlines disclosed donating $2.5 million in March.

And RTX, the defense company formerly known as Raytheon, reported giving $1.5 million in May.

Chevron, United Airlines and RTX are among the nearly two-dozen corporate sponsors listed on the Freedom 250 website.

“As a proud American company, Chevron is pleased to support celebrations of 250 years of the country's independence,” Bill Turenne, a spokesperson, told NOTUS.

United Airlines declined to comment. RTX did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for Palantir, one of the companies listed as a sponsor on the website, told NOTUS the company did not donate to Freedom 250.

“Palantir is proud to adhere to all lobbying and donation disclosure requirements, but the company did not make a contribution to Freedom 250,” the Palantir spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement.

GE Aerospace declined to comment. UnitedHealth Group, John Deere, Lockheed Martin, TikTok, Oracle, ExxonMobil, Northrop Grumman, ScottsMiracle-Gro, Exiger, Mosaic and SAP did not respond to requests for comment from NOTUS.

Other companies not listed by Freedom 250 as official partners or sponsors said they did not pay the organization money despite having their corporate logos posted around the Great American State Fair.

Axiom Space had an exhibit that included a video and a large astronaut cutout. But Meridyth Moore, a spokesperson for Axiom Space, said the company “was not a paid sponsor.”
Axiom.Space (8064x4536, AR: 1.78)"That’s it. We provided a cutout image of our spacesuit and a video to be played,” Moore responded when asked for more details about the exhibit.

When NOTUS asked if the organizers had allowed Axiom to include the pieces for free, Moore confirmed “no expenditures were spent.”

Hillsdale College, a small, Christian liberal arts school in Michigan, also had a branded booth at the Great American State Fair. Emily Davis, a college spokesperson, described Hillsdale as a “partner” but said the college did not donate to Freedom 250.

“The college complies with all reporting obligations. It has not given any monies to the Freedom 250 group,” Davis said.

SAP, a business software company, operated a large exhibit at the Great American State Fair, which included a display wall featuring the logos of several client companies alongside QR codes and a rotating digital display detailing some of the brands.
SAP.ads.Great.American.State.Fair (8044x4525, AR: 1.78)Todd Scott, senior communications manager at Hershey, one of the companies featured in the SAP exhibit, told NOTUS that the chocolate company was not a sponsor and that this was the first he had heard about the company’s logo being on the SAP exhibit at the Great American State Fair. (NOTUS reported on Hershey’s presence at the Great American State Fair in July.)

Scott pointed to an article in The Philadelphia Inquirer, where he previously said Hershey was “asked so late in the game” to participate in the Great American State Fair that the company could not logistically participate.

Funding for Freedom 250 has often lacked transparency since the group began operating alongside America250 — a separate nonprofit group supporting the U.S. Semiquincentennial Commission, which Congress established a decade ago.

Oil company BP, for one, disclosed a $500,000 contribution to America250 in February, according to its latest contribution report filed last Friday.

Democrats on the House Natural Resources Committee accused Freedom 250 of diverting funds from America250, including by allegedly giving donors the routing and account numbers for Freedom 250, according to a report released by the committee last month.

Freedom 250 spokesperson Danielle Alvarez previously told NPR that the claims are "categorically false” and a "partisan smear."

"Congressional members should be ashamed they are spending countless hours fabricating a report instead of joining Americans in creating an absolutely beautiful celebration," Alvarez told NPR last month.

Alvarez did not immediately respond to a NOTUS message following up on questions emailed separately to Freedom 250.

entries.title: Do the Commanders have a problem at center?
entries.summary: With presumed starter Nick Allegretti sidelined, the position has drawn attention early in camp.
entries.content:
Things are looking a little dicey at the center of the Commanders’ offensive line.

The team’s presumed starter at the center position is actually a converted guard. His backup is also a converted guard. The rookie they drafted in the sixth round of April’s draft — a converted guard. The center they signed earlier this week to fill in due to injuries? You guessed it.

As the Commanders make their way through the second week of training camp, the centers have drawn a fair amount of attention. With the offense seeking to rebound from a bottom-10 performance last season, it's unclear what one of the unit’s most important positions will look like next week, let alone next month.

Coach Dan Quinn isn’t in panic mode. Despite the absence of starter Nick Allegretti due to a calf strain, Quinn said the offensive line has held up.

“Both sides of the line I thought had, you know, advantage here, advantage there, and that's what I'm hoping to see,” he said ahead of practice Tuesday. “If one gets tilted too much to the other, then I'd be more concerned. So I like the back-and-forth, honestly, to say good run here, good blitz there.”

Despite Quinn’s optimistic take, there are still plenty of question marks. Allegretti has not practiced since July 29. His backup, Julian Good-Jones, has had an up-and-down run as fill-in with the first team, including one snap that went over Jayden Daniels’ head during team drills on Tuesday. Rookie Matt Gulbin has rolled almost exclusively with the second team, but depth is clearly a concern.

The team worked out centers Gus Hartwig, Joe Michalski and Trey Hill on Saturday. Hill, a sixth-round pick by the Bengals in 2021 who played guard early in college, was signed the following day. Following Saturday’s and Monday’s practices, guards Timothy McKay and Brandon Coleman and tackle Trent Scott stayed to take snaps with Marcus Mariota.

Quinn said all the maneuvering has been aimed at building depth (before Hill’s arrival Gulbin was the only player on the team roster listed as a center), but is also an experiment to see who is capable of handling center responsibilities.

“If you can play inside, you want somebody that can play both [center and guard],” Quinn said. “And that's basically kind of the rhythm behind it.”

The center position is pivotal to the offense. The job isn’t solely about successfully snapping the ball to the quarterback. Centers are responsible for calling out defensive alignments, coordinating blocking assignments and, of course, handling the defender in front of them.

And yet Washington has not had consistency at the position for years. Since 2021, at least 10 players have taken snaps at center for Washington. Last season, the offensive line was just about average in ESPN’s pass- and run-block metrics, and that was before starting center Tyler Biadasz was released in February.

Quinn has commended Gulbin for his command of the second unit line.

“I think it's just kind of a next-man-up mentality,” Gulbin said. “I have to step up to the plate and make sure the O line's functioning, and I'm getting out calls.”

Allegretti has helped coach up Good-Jones and Gulbin from the sideline. Those three, and now Hill, can be seen bouncing ideas and techniques off one another. After practice they often put in extra work with assistant offensive line coach Shane Toub.

“I come off the sideline, he's [Allegretti’s] helping me out with ‘Oh, what was this? What was this look?’ We break it down together,” Good-Jones said. “So it's a brotherhood, man. It's a collaborative unit.”

Quinn has said he doesn’t expect Allegretti to be out much longer. And even though the seven-year veteran started just one game at center for Washington last season, his teammates, the coaching staff and front office have raved about him.

“What stands out to me with Nick is just his leadership, his command, his confidence, the way the guys gravitate to and listen to him,” general manager Adam Peters said at a press conference before camp. “And so that's a big part of it. Knowing what to do, knowing where to go, knowing where to direct the guys, just the calling up in the huddle — it's a big deal.”

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Aug. 7)
entries.summary: The grand opening of Olney Theatre’s expansion, a sitcom-inspired dance party, and a canine competition at the Wharf.
entries.content:
Thursday

“Woody Guthrie’s American Song,” Theatre Alliance at Wharf Park
515 Water St. SW, 7:15 p.m., pay what you can

One of D.C.’s buzziest theater companies opens a three-month, citywide festival of performances and exhibits celebrating “America's most enduring folk poet and social agitator.” Expect more than a “This Land Is Your Land” sing-along at this outdoor musical revue that addresses America’s turbulent social climate through the lens of Guthrie’s writings and songs. Recommended for fans of Bob Dylan, Pete Seeger and Rhiannon Giddens.

Rip! Tear! Collage Exhibit at Eye Street Gallery
200 I St. SE, 6 p.m. free

The D.C. Commission on the Arts and Humanities picked “Collage as Critique” as the theme for its annual juried show, which awards grants to artists whose work is chosen for display. More than 20 local artists have work in the 2026 exhibit, and three of them will be on hand to lead a workshop on shredding, tearing and ripping up paper, then turning the scraps into art.

More to explore: “Apollo 13” blasts off at the Library of Congress’ Movies on the Lawn.

Friday

“Tosca” at Wolf Trap
1551 Trap Road, Vienna, Va., 8 p.m., $39 to $107

The Washington National Opera Orchestra — a beleaguered group of veteran musicians who were recently kicked out of the Kennedy Center — will accompany up-and-coming singers on the Wolf Trap stage. The summer company produces one major opera each year, and this season it’s Puccini’s classic about an artist, his muse and the religious zealot police chief out to thwart their star-crossed romance. Husband-and-wife team Ryan and Tonya McKinny, who have vocally opposed President Trump’s Kennedy Center takeover, will direct the production and provide subtext, while José Luis Gómez conducts.

“SUNNY RAVE” at the Howard Theatre
620 T St., 10 p.m., $30

New York and Toronto may have “Heated Rivalry” parody musicals, but D.C. has [checks notes] a late-night “Always Sunny in Philadelphia” dance party? Yep. That’s a thing. The Philadelphia-based “dj pressed” will spin tunes accompanied by clips from the long-running FX comedy at the Howard Theatre. Come dressed as Mac, Dee or Danny DeVito.

More to explore: Country singer Jordan Davis performs a free show for ticketholders after the Nationals game.

Saturday

Chesapeake DogDocks at The Wharf
101 District Square SW, 10:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., free

Come watch Prince, Banana and their canine frenemies play fetch in a 40-foot pool installed outside The Anthem. Billed as the mid-Atlantic’s premiere “aquatic dog performance” club, the Chesapeake DockDogs are hosting their first District competition surrounded by bougie people drinking beer. (Cerveza Pacifico and Tito’s “Vodka for Dog People” are the event sponsors.) Think your pooch might have what it takes to take the big leap next year? The club is organizing a “Youth Day” introductory session in Marriottsville, Md., on Aug. 15, minus the pool and booze.

Crochet Community Social at Museum of Contemporary Art Arlington
525 14th St. S, Arlington, Va., 2:30 to 4 p.m., free

Bring your own needles or pick up a free pair at this informal gathering hosted by the Crochet Cart Project. Participants will each contribute a square for a community blanket. That may sound more wholesome than trad-wife Instagram, but the group also aims to spread the joy of crocheting to all communities and help people express “creativity through fibre art.”

More to explore: Swing Fling dance convention at the Dulles Hyatt Regency; Sneaker Con at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center.

Sunday

Summerfest Open House at Olney Theatre
2001 Olney-Sandy Spring Road, Olney, Md., 11:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., free

Families in the Northern suburbs (and anyone else who loves theater and has a car) are likely to love the grand opening of Olney Theatre Center’s multimillion-dollar expansion project. After two years of construction, the 88-year-old Montgomery County theater has a new lobby, studios and education spaces. More than two-dozen free shows, tours and workshops are on the schedule, while food trucks and a used costume shop are open all day. A gala performance featuring “Younger” star and Tony-winner Sutton Foster caps off the celebration, but tickets have long been sold out.

Mandoleers at Lyon Park Community Center
414 N. Fillmore Street, Arlington, Va., 5 p.m., free

Since 1923, the Mandoleers have been making music together on instruments that resemble miniature guitars. The ensemble holds a three-day intensive each summer, open to anyone who plays the mandolin, mandola, mandocello, classical guitar or upright bass. It’s unclear how exactly this merry band of musicians will celebrate the Declaration of Independence, but the event culminates with a free community concert called, “America at 250: We the People, All of Us.” Ernesto Parets conducts.

More to explore: Final weekend to see the critically hailed “American Aspirations” exhibit at the Smithsonian Institution Building.

Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: A drop in Metro crime, $1.4 billion for the National Guard and a confusing Nats trade deadline. 





THE LATEST

Crime on Metro has hit a “new historic low.”

New crime data released by WMATA shows that Part I crimes — more serious offenses like assaults, robberies and thefts — are down 12% since last year and 61% since 2023.

The consistent decreases in crime come from cops, cameras and compassion, says WMATA general manager Randy Clarke. There are more police officers and security guards patrolling stations and buses; 30,000 cameras are monitoring the system; and low-income riders are offered discounts to help prevent fare evasion.

Clarke said Tuesday the drop in crime and increase in ridership have created something of a virtuous cycle for Metro, with safer trains and buses encouraging ridership, and more riders putting more eyes to work. “Not only is [Metro] much safer, it’s much safer for a lot more people,” he said. (Even still, ridership numbers remain below where they were pre-pandemic.)

Fare evasion enforcement has been a particular focus for Metro in recent years. Clarke said enforcement on trains increased 485% from 2023 to 2026. Ramped-up enforcement on buses that was launched this year has led to a 1,371% spike in citations.

Clarke himself has even gotten in on enforcing the rules. He said he recently stopped an older man who tried to get into a Metro station using one of the Kids Ride Free cards that are handed out to schoolchildren in the city. (Note to self: Don’t use your kids’ cards.)

Still, there have been snags. NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle recently reported that a bureaucratic snafu has led to most fare-evasion citations issued in D.C. being dismissed. Clarke says he wants a regional solution to ensure that fare evasion is prosecuted consistently across the Metro system.

President Donald Trump plans to spend $1.4 billion in taxpayer funds keeping the National Guard in D.C. until January 2029, NOTUS’ Angie Orellana Hernandez reports.

The eye-popping estimate, provided to Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s office and shared with NOTUS, includes a recently announced $292 million contract to keep troops housed through the end of Trump’s term.

For context: The D.C. police department’s annual budget for its 3,100 officers is roughly $600 million.

The left-leaning Free D.C. Slate swept up 75% of the seats up for grabs on the D.C. Democratic State Committee, ousting the committee’s more moderate members, The Washington Post reports.

JBG Smith — a real estate investment trust with a massive footprint in the DMV — delayed its earnings report after a D.C. Superior Court judge ordered last week that the company pay $356 million to a condo association, the Washington Business Journal reports. The condo owners sued in 2020, alleging defects in their building’s elevators, roof, HVAC system, electrical system, exterior walls, parking garage elevators and foundation.

JBG Smith has about $2.6 billion in debt and has reported 12 straight quarterly losses. NOTUS previously reported on abysmal conditions at another property it co-owns: The Gale Eckington.





FROM MARYLAND

Montgomery County’s gun laws are in the Trump administration’s crosshairs. This week, the Justice Department sued the county over a law it says makes it “practically impossible for individuals in the county to go about their daily business while lawfully carrying a firearm.” Late last year, the DOJ similarly filed suit against D.C. over the city’s ban on AR-15 assault rifles.


FROM VIRGINIA

Virginia’s health department is investigating the state’s first documented case of locally acquired dengue virus. The disease is spread through infected mosquitoes, but officials said the public’s risk of acquiring it is low.

The Nationals took a hybrid approach to the trade deadline, which meant selling key players to add a bunch of new pitchers — a few of whom could help the team this season. But since there was still more selling for the future than buying for the present, the deadline felt familiar to fans who are tired of rooting for a team that keeps trading away some of its best talent every summer, NOTUS' Jesse Dougherty writes.

The Freedom 250 IndyCar race taking place in the District this month will be longer than anticipated: Officials announced this week that the race will be extended from 122 laps to 147 so it can hit the 250-mile mark.

entries.title: A House Candidate Who Dropped Out Beats Trump's Pick in Michigan
entries.summary: Amir Hassan lost by double-digit percentage points to Thomas J. Smith, who accepted the nomination despite dropping out of the race last month.
entries.content:
A Michigan Republican endorsed by President Donald Trump lost his primary election to a candidate who dropped out of the race but remained on the ballot, the Associated Press projected Wednesday.

Amir Hassan, a former federal law enforcement officer from Flint, Michigan, trailed retired engineer Thomas J. Smith by about 17 percentage points. Smith suspended his campaign to represent Michigan’s 8th Congressional District in July.

The pair were vying to flip the seat held by Democratic incumbent Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet.

Trump-endorsed candidates have won about 97% of their primary elections in 2026, according to a July 10 review by Ballotpedia. Hassan is the only Trump-backed House candidate in Michigan who lost his primary.

Trump brought Hassan and other candidates onstage during a rally in Michigan on July 27, where the president made reference to Hassan’s family ties to industry giant General Motors. At the rally, Hassan told attendees that they were putting “this country back on the map because we have a leader who stands up for us.”

Hassan acknowledged his apparent defeat in the early hours on Wednesday.

“The fight has just begun,” Hassan wrote on X. “Service never stops.”

Smith accepted the nomination in a statement early Wednesday to The Detroit News. He said he was “humbled and honored that Republicans have chosen me to take the fight to Kristen McDonald Rivet."

“I look forward to working with Speaker Johnson and the entire Republican team to expand our House majority and advance President Trump’s America First agenda to lower costs for working families and make America affordable again,” Smith added.

The Michigan Secretary of State’s office did not immediately reply to a request for comment on whether Smith can proceed with his nomination despite his decision to officially withdraw from the race.

After dropping out, Smith had backed another candidate, Al Lemmo, who came in last with about 16.4% of the vote.

McDonald Rivet ran unopposed in her Democratic primary election.

entries.title: Michigan Hands the Democratic Establishment Another Brutal Loss
entries.summary: Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow win is a low point for the center-left as Democrats head toward November.
entries.content:
Democrats will remember 2026 as the year their party’s establishment lost its once total control of the primary process.

Instead, it was outmaneuvered and overwhelmed by a progressive insurgency whose chosen candidates, backed by a furious liberal base, smashed their way to victories.

It’s a low point for the center-left that Democratic leaders can climb out of, party strategists say, but only with a radical readjustment of how they operate.

The result of Michigan’s Senate Democratic primary Tuesday — in which outspoken progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens — was arguably the sharpest blow yet. Stevens lost despite having a huge cash advantage, outspending him 11-to-1 in ads, and running a playbook that had worked for moderate candidates for years, including during Hillary Clinton’s and Joe Biden’s presidential campaigns. El-Sayed winning only narrowly, despite his own campaign’s expectations of a blowout victory, just poses more questions of what if anything the party establishment could’ve done differently to head off the rising left.

The choice to support Stevens was emblematic of a larger problem with how party leaders anoint candidates, said some Democratic strategists, and a failure to properly understand just how angry their own party’s voters were with the old way of conducting politics.

“They value seniority over talent, a fundraising rolodex over ability to make genuine voter connections, institutional comfort over the anger and change that voters are actually demanding,” said Lis Smith, a veteran Democratic strategist who worked for a candidate in the race who dropped out, Mallory McMorrow. “If you put up establishment slop against DSA candidates who may have bad ideas but are exciting and speak to the anger of American voters, Democratic voters are going to choose DSA and far-left candidates, until we get our act together.”

Democratic voters, said another party strategist, were “shouting from the rooftops” about their anger.

“If we don’t actually respect and respond to this frustration, we’re gonna wind up with heads in a basket,” said the party operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly.

Democratic Party leaders counter that they have mostly gotten their way in primaries this year and more importantly, could be poised for a big midterm election in November in part because of successful candidate recruitment. Democratic Senate candidates from Texas to North Carolina lead in public polling as President Donald Trump’s approval rating sags to all-time lows. Gas prices are still high, and voters say they’re still feeling the cost-of-living pinch. Those environmental factors have put not just the House in play but also the Senate, an unlikely possibility just two years ago.

Both the Democratic National Committee and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee quickly rallied around El-Sayed after his win. DSCC chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and Democratic Senate leader Sen. Chuck Schumer said in a statement that El-Sayed had “inspired thousands of Michiganders” and that the party is united behind him.

But Tuesday’s result in Michigan was only the latest setback for Democrats in Washington this year. In June, Maine Gov. Janet Mills lost her primary race in an embarrassing landslide to political newcomer Graham Platner, despite an endorsement from the DSCC. (Platner later exited the race.) Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado failed to clinch his gubernatorial race, which revolved around his closeness to Washington leadership.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has lost three races in California, Arizona and Maine, where it spent money on its preferred candidate. The party has also seen progressive candidates win some House races in which the party establishment split its support among multiple candidates. That happened again on Tuesday night in Michigan, where progressive activist Will Lawrence beat two moderates in a swing district.

And a handful of incumbent Democratic House members, from Colorado to New York, have lost their reelection races to Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated candidates, a rarity in a party that traditionally has valued its incumbents.

“It’s not the end of the center-left, but they need to do a better job of consolidating earlier rather than letting multiple go in the same lane," said Kevin McKeon, a Democratic strategist who works on Senate and House races.

Of course, establishment Democrats still have successes to claim this cycle. Of the 13 candidates on the DCCC’s coveted Red to Blue endorsement list, 10 have won their respective primaries. The DSCC recruited former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown and former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola into their respective Senate races without any incident, instantly putting the trio of states into play. In Iowa, the establishment-backed candidate, state Rep. Josh Turek, also won a contested primary.

That’s something DSCC aides are all too happy to point out.

“Senate Democrats created a path to win a majority thanks to all-star candidate recruitment, formidable campaigns, and a winning message,” Tommy Garcia, a DSCC spokesperson, said in a statement. “Democratic candidates are out-polling and out-raising their Republican opponents, and in November we will win the majority — which no one thought was possible a year ago.”

Democrats are even more bullish on taking the House majority than the Senate, in part because of investments in many key races.

“Everyone agrees that the stakes could not be higher for November,” Viet Shelton, a DCCC spokesperson, said in a statement. ”The DCCC is doing everything possible to ensure Democrats win the biggest majority possible and Congress can actually deliver for the American people again. Every poll is proving we are (still) well positioned to do just that.”

Center-left Democrats are quick to point to November as the ultimate scorecard for the wings of the party.

“It's worth remembering,” said a Democratic consultant granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly, that progressive won primaries in Omaha, Nebraska, and Syracuse, New York, a pair of battleground House districts. But Democrats “went on to win the majority in 2018 without winning either of the Omaha or Syracuse seats.”

Some Democratic leaders expressed optimism that the party losing some primaries was ultimately good — that it could help expose leaders in Congress to new ideas and energy.

“I actually think this is a healthy debate to have,” said Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who has endorsed candidates running against the party establishment this year and previously served as the chair of both the DCCC and DSCC. “I think we need this kind of churning in the Democratic Party.”

Even so, party leaders have problems beyond this year’s primaries. Schumer has faced calls from some candidates and activists to step aside, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been on the receiving end of frustration from some activists and candidates. Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin has been beset by crises since taking over last year, dogged by controversy over the party’s fundraising tactics and a botched 2024 autopsy report.

And Michigan isn’t the last crucial test the party will face this primary cycle. In Wisconsin, a democratic socialist candidate is favored to win the gubernatorial primary next week, in part because other Democratic candidates failed to consolidate support or gain traction.

“Since I've been paying attention to politics, the Democratic Party has never been as weak and unpopular as it is now,” said Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, a liberal grassroots group. “And I think that’s just an empirical fact.”

Levin has been critical of Democratic Party leadership since Trump’s inauguration last year, arguing they haven’t been forceful or creative enough in their opposition to the president. He, like others interviewed for this story, said he thought the base’s frustration with party leadership was more about its failure to defeat Trump in 2024 and the perception it has done little to thwart him while in office.

Even among Democrats who have represented battleground districts, there’s a concern the party isn’t offering “bigger, bolder policy ideas this year” and the party hasn’t “been inspiring enough,” said former Rep. Susan Wild.

“Voters are looking for [an] actual strategy for how we are going to be different, what our plan is,” Wild said, citing “Medicare for All” and subsidized child care as potential policy platforms. “You can’t just talk about an affordability agenda without talking specifics.”

During the second Trump administration, Danielle Butterfield, president of Democratic super PAC Priorities USA, voters have identified a “vacuum in Democratic leadership.”

“In a world where our party doesn't have any lever of government, our leadership is failing in crazy ways,” Butterfield said. “It has created this circular firing squad of everyone else saying, ‘Maybe someone else will step up.’ And progressive Democrats are the ones who are meeting the moment, and people want that.”

Butterfield pointed to the difference she saw in the ads from El-Sayed’s and Stevens’ campaigns. She believed El-Sayed did a better job explaining to voters exactly how he proposed to make their lives better, centered on passing “Medicare for All” and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“As a whole, progressive candidates are meeting that anger more vividly,” she said. “And we're seeing that play out in these primaries.”

entries.title: Rep. Shri Thanedar Loses Reelection Bid to DSA-Backed Challenger
entries.summary: He narrowly lost his primary to state Rep. Donavan McKinney.
entries.content:
Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar lost his reelection bid to a progressive challenger after two terms representing Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, the Associated Press projected Wednesday.

Thanedar, who admitted to NOTUS this week that he struggled to garner support from his congressional colleagues, was down by 4 percentage points to state Rep. Donavan McKinney with nearly all of the votes counted.

Thanedar conceded in a statement Wednesday, adding his name to the slate of incumbent Democrats who lost their primary to candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America and other progressive groups.

“It was a tough election cycle and, in the end, the voters of the 13th District chose him to represent them moving forward,” Thanedar said of McKinney, a lifelong resident of Detroit.

Several members of the Congressional Black Caucus also backed McKinney to represent the 13th District, an area with a large population of Black residents.

McKinney campaigned on “Medicare for All,” a Green New Deal and ending military aid to Israel — a topic that loomed over Democratic primaries in Michigan. McKinney previously told NOTUS he saw constituents’ economic struggles as inseparable from the federal government funding Israel’s attacks on Palestinians and working alongside Tel Aviv on a “war for no reason with Iran [that costs] $1 billion per day.”

“People around the country are just tired of status-quo politicians,” McKinney told NOTUS.

The DSA endorsed McKinney in July, saying he would “fight for strong union jobs, environmental justice and for universal childcare.”

Thanedar, a retired entrepreneur and scientist, largely self-funded his reelection campaign. He had picked up endorsements from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and Reps. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi) and Cleo Fields (D-Louisiana).

When previously asked by NOTUS if he wished he had more congressional support, Thanedar said, “No, no, I have plenty.”

“It’s not like a high school,” Thanedar said. “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress.”

entries.title: Trump’s Helicopter Involved in Air-Traffic Safety Incident
entries.summary: The White House said “at no point was the President in harm’s way,” but federal aviation officials are reviewing the incident.
entries.content:
The Federal Aviation Administration is looking into a safety incident involving President Donald Trump’s helicopter and air-traffic control at a nearby airport.

When Marine One — the call sign for the aircraft carrying the president — took off from the White House on Tuesday, air-traffic controllers had not halted flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport as required by federal aviation standards, The Wall Street Journal first reported.

The incident triggered what the FAA calls a loss of standard separation, potentially placing Marine One closer than the acceptable range between aircraft required by federal aviation rules: 1.5 miles horizontally and 500 feet vertically.

“Based on our preliminary safety review, there was momentary loss of separation after which the aircraft continued to move away from one another,” the FAA told NOTUS in an emailed statement. “The air traffic controller was in contact with both the commercial pilot and Marine One pilot during the loss of separation.”

FAA officials are “continuing to review the incident and will implement any appropriate corrective actions” based on their evaluation.

“Marine One flights are piloted by some of the best aviators in the world, and at no point was the President in harm’s way,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai wrote in a statement.

Federal aviation officials created new rules for air-traffic control safety after a deadly crash between an American Airlines passenger plane and a military Black Hawk helicopter killed 67 people on Jan. 29, 2025. The two aircraft collided midair and crashed into the Potomac River near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

The National Transportation Safety Board found a collection of “systemic failures in airspace design, safety oversight, and risk management” by the FAA and the U.S. Army at fault for the midair collision. The NTSB made 33 safety recommendations to the FAA, which included defining a “close proximity encounter” and maintaining a public database to monitor these events.

entries.content:
Today’s notice: Hope you wanted the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan to go on longer. Max Miller says he has friends in high places. Latest on Todd Blanche’s nomination. Redistricting’s next steps. Private health info leaked with Fauci’s journal. And: Bond market warning signs.





THE LATEST

The dreaded third option: When the polls closed in Michigan last night, the idea was that Democrats would get clarity on the questions that have plagued them throughout the primary season. A big win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed would mean the left could fight off big outside money and wave off pesky worries about electability. A clear win by Rep. Haley Stevens, the establishment pick, would signal that battleground Democrats weren’t ready to take the same ideological risks as safely blue places — and let party leadership breathe a little.

El-Sayed remains ahead of Stevens, but the margin is too narrow for there to be a clear winner early this morning. That means the argument about the party’s future goes on.

It was a proverbial Groundhog Day for this Democratic primary cycle, and the little guy saw his shadow — forecasting at least six more weeks of Democratic Party angst. Bring on the Wisconsin primary!

One thing we definitely learned last night: time to really stop listening to the polls, right? There were a lot of them in this Senate primary and in most cases they were, uh, not accurate.

Jeff Flake backs Jon Ossoff (AJC); Arizona’s Democratic Governor Set to Pick a Republican Running Mate (NYT)





From the Hill


Rep. Max Miller says he has allies: The embattled Ohio Republican vowed to stay in his reelection race, called for a House Ethics investigation of his conduct and asserted powerful people still have his back, NOTUS’ Adora Brown writes. “Speaker Mike Johnson, everyone else, they’re standing behind me,” Miller told CNN. “No one has told me to get off the ballot.” Johnson hasn’t publicly joined calls for Miller to step down and didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Todd Blanche drama gets one more act: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said yesterday that she’ll vote against Blanche, Trump’s nominee to be attorney general. That means Blanche must win over at least one of the two remaining Republican holdouts in the Senate to be confirmed, NOTUS’ Al Weaver reports. The senators to watch: Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Bill Cassidy (R-Lousiana).


From the redistricting wars


Redistricting rekindled: Maryland statehouse Democrats passed a constitutional amendment yesterday that would make it easier to redraw congressional lines ahead of the 2028 election, NOTUS’ Manuela Silva reports. And 900 miles away in Missouri, the state’s top elections official blocked a petition challenging a Republican-passed map aimed at eliminating Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s seat.

THE BIG ONE


Rand Paul’s doxing problem: When the Kentucky senator made public the journal kept by Anthony Fauci last week, Paul also released personal medical information of more than 20 individuals, NOTUS’ Margaret Manto reports.

What’s included: Names, diagnoses, symptoms and test results of individuals. Two of the people identified by name alongside their medical details were children, Margaret writes. (One of those was the child of Trumpworld players Stephen and Katie Miller, as we first reported.) Some are very public figures like Joe Biden, and others appear to be private individuals whose medical history was posted for the world to see.

And those individuals are understandably angry. “If I was a victimizer in the Epstein files, my name would have been redacted,” Leslie Adelman, whose name and medical condition were posted in the document dump, told NOTUS. (Adelman gave permission to use her name in Margaret’s story.) “Instead, I am an innocent and productive member of society, who has donated her time and body to NIH for research that will benefit millions of people — yet MY name and information is blasted to the national news.”

NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

When Trump called Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz “seriously retarded” last year, it was part of a disturbing pattern. “The use of slurs in general is up,” according to one expert. “But nothing comes near the numbers we’re seeing on the R-word.” Today at NOTUS Perspectives, Sadie Dingfelder explains why this particular insult has become the defining slur of the Trump era.

NOTUS’ Igor Bobic is joined by Avani Kalra and Al Weaver to discuss the inner machinations of the Senate Republican Conference and President Trump’s “dog with a chew toy” focus on the voting act.

Bad signs in the bond market: Last week’s unexpected surge in bond yields — primarily triggered by doubts about the Fed’s commitment to fighting inflation — could hit small- and medium-sized banks hard if the market doesn’t calm, NOTUS’ Jeff Stein reports. The implications for the U.S. economy, not to mention the midterms, are potentially huge. Volatility in the bond markets helped push Trump to back off of his “Liberation Day” tariff scheme, which corrected the situation quickly. But the spike this time was less sudden and has gotten less attention, Jeff writes, and it may also be harder to resolve.

entries.title: Darline Graham Takes Over Lindsey Graham’s Leadership PAC
entries.summary: The newly inaugurated senator is now listed as a “leadership PAC sponsor” for her late brother’s well-funded political committee.
entries.content:
Sen. Darline Graham just inherited an unconventional asset from her deceased brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham: his federal leadership PAC.

Federal records reviewed by NOTUS now list Darline Graham as Fund for America’s Future’s sponsor. Filings from earlier this year listed Lindsey Graham as the PAC’s sponsor.

Such a sibling-to-sibling transfer of a senator’s political action committee is decidedly uncommon.

“There's little official guidance from the FEC specifically addressing the transfer of a leadership PAC after the death of its sponsoring lawmaker,” Michael Beckel, the director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a nonpartisan political reform organization, told NOTUS. “In practice, most leadership PACs associated with deceased or retired lawmakers are eventually wound down or terminated rather than transferred to another politician.”

After Lindsey Graham died last month at the age of 71, the treasurer of the leadership PAC — long-time Republican operative Cabell Hobbs — could have moved to wind down the committee and dispose of any remaining funds by donating to certain political committees and charitable organizations or refunding donors, according to FEC rules.

Hobbs declined to comment on the matter when reached by phone Wednesday.

Darline Graham’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the sponsorship transfer.

Although Darline Graham inheriting both her late brother’s Senate seat and leadership fund is unique, it is “not surprising” because “the stars aligned in this case,” Beckel said.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to serve the remainder of her brother’s term, and she decided to seek a full term after President Donald Trump told her to run.
Graham Trump (2676x1784, AR: 1.50)During the 2026 election cycle, Fund for America’s Future has raised more than $632,000 through a variety of donations and cash transfers, FEC records indicate. It ended June with about $70,000 cash on hand after having spent much of what it’s recently raised.

It is incredibly common for lawmakers to have leadership PACs; 96% of the 119th Congress — 511 out of 531 members — have leadership committees, per Issue One. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) is the only senator who does not have this type of PAC. The committees allow lawmakers to donate to other campaigns, which builds their political network.

“Money in the leadership PAC helps you buy friends and allies, so being able to raise money and dole that out to other politicians is a way for her to be helpful to the team,” Beckel said.

But Fund for America’s Future isn’t the only PAC that’s thrown its support behind Darline Graham.

The Security is Strength super PAC, which has been affiliated with several committees supporting Lindsey Graham, has pledged millions to bolster his sister’s campaign. The committee announced a $100,000 digital ad buy for Darline Graham on Wednesday, with TV spots attacking one of her opponents, Rep. Russell Fry (R-South Carolina).

Republicans in South Carolina will have the chance to vote for a new nominee in a special election on Aug. 11, because Lindsey Graham had already won the nomination for his party in June.

Darline Graham is set to face Rep. Ralph Norman, former Rep. and Gov. Mark Sanford, businessman Mark Lynch and Fry in the special election. Whoever advances will be running against Democratic opponent pediatrician Annie Andrews in the general election in November.

entries.title: Congress’ Watchdog Is Still Struggling to Get Answers on DOGE
entries.summary: The Trump administration isn’t handing over records of DOGE staffers completing training, ethics disclosures.
entries.content:
The White House says DOGE employees were trained on ethics and how to manage government records, but won’t give Congress’ watchdog the receipts to back that up.

The Government Accountability Office released a report Wednesday claiming that the White House, Elon Musk and government agencies did not fully cooperate with its oversight investigation, leaving basic questions about how DOGE operated unanswered over a year after the government-slashing group began its work.

DOGE’s work pushing government employees out of their jobs, cutting government spending and pressing for high-level access to government data and systems repeatedly sparked ethics, privacy and records concerns.

The GAO asked the White House and 25 federal agencies for information on DOGE personnel who were employed by the Executive Office of the President through the end of this January. That’s already a subset of the total number of associates who worked for DOGE, as some were employed by other agencies.

In response, nine agencies sent back detailed information on about 60 DOGE employees. The watchdog group, using public information and court filings, identified nearly 150 other DOGE personnel in total.

Ten agencies — including ones that were early focuses for DOGE, such as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the U.S. Agency for International Development, which Musk’s team dismantled — didn’t provide the GAO with any information. Others said they didn’t have DOGE employees. The White House provided responses to some questions from the GAO, but didn’t hand over any documentation or respond to requests for interviews.

The GAO mailed Musk a letter at Tesla headquarters asking for information about his position in the White House and with DOGE. He didn’t respond. Last year, the administration initially said Musk was in charge of the cost-cutting effort only to later pivot and say that a previously low-profile government bureaucrat, Amy Gleason, was the acting DOGE administrator.

The GAO also sent a letter to a senior policy advisor at Tesla's Washington, D.C., office.

“Both letters were signed for upon delivery,” a footnote in the watchdog’s report reads. “We did not receive responses to either letter.”

The GAO did find that among the agencies that did respond, “completion statuses” for required training and financial disclosures “varied by agency,” the report says.

Those agencies told the GAO that 49 of the approximately 60 reported DOGE employees had completed ethics training, something that an employee’s “home agency” is responsible for. DOGE regularly detailed employees from one agency to another.

The White House — the home agency for most of the DOGE employees the GAO was investigating as part of this report — said that “DOGE personnel who held positions within EOP receive the same ethics training as all other EOP personnel.”

But it “did not respond to our requests for documentation showing whether individual DOGE personnel completed ethics training,” the GAO wrote.

Agencies told the watchdog that 18 of the roughly 60 DOGE staffers had done records-management training. At the General Services Administration, a DOGE stronghold, only three of the 21 DOGE employees were marked as having completed records-management training in government documentation.

The GAO also reviewed financial disclosure reports — which are required for federal employees whose roles involve the potential for conflicts of interest — for 38 of the approximately 60 DOGE-ers it received information on from agencies. The White House wouldn’t provide copies of these reports, the watchdog said.

At least a few DOGE associates appear not to have filed reports at all. The GSA told the GAO that two of its DOGE associates left before the disclosures were due at the 30-day mark of their work.

“The Administration continues to keep the American people in the dark, refusing to answer basic questions,” Rep. Richard Neal (D-Massachusetts), one of the lawmakers who asked the GAO to conduct this oversight report, told NOTUS in a statement.

The Trump administration has a history of stonewalling Congress’ watchdog agency, as NOTUS has previously reported. Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, has long sparred with the GAO and even said he doesn’t think the congressional oversight office should exist at all.

“The vast majority of agencies continue to cooperate with GAO,” Sarah Kaczmarek, the watchdog group’s managing director of public affairs, told NOTUS in a statement. “But timely cooperation from federal agencies is essential to ensuring Congress has the information it needs to conduct effective oversight.”

entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for August 5, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!




THE LATEST

Michigan finally has its Democratic Senate nominee in Abdul El-Sayed, whose razor-thin race was called this morning after weeks of touting expectations for a blowout victory. His previous opponents, Rep. Haley Stevens and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, have lined up behind him.

What do his potential colleagues think? A quick search among Michigan Dems shows only Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet and Sen. Elissa Slotkin’s personal X accounts have congratulated El-Sayed by name today. Rep. Hillary Scholten’s personal account issued a congratulatory statement that did not name the Senate nominee.

  • Retiring Michigan Sen. Gary Peters — who says he’ll back El-Sayed — bashed reporting that showed the candidate up by double digits based on internal polling. He told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic it was a “technique as old politics itself. We saw polls that were questionable right from the start for me.”
The NSRC put up its first attack ad today, calling him “Abdulrahman Muhammad El-Sayed — the most radical Senate candidate in America.”

  • “That’s the only play they got,” El-Sayed told voters this morning. “My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war.”




THE HILL

The allegations against Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) prompted different statements from the House’s two women’s caucuses. Democrats called for his resignation, while Republican Women’s Caucus Chair Kat Cammack said she respected the Ethics Committee’s need to follow due process.

  • Cammack, who is working to tackle workplace sexual misconduct on the Hill, called the situation “painful” for everyone involved: “My heart especially breaks for the little girl caught in the middle.”
The Senate confirmed CDC director nominee Erica Schwartz, the agency’s first permanent director in nearly a year.





THE ADMINISTRATION

Donald Trump’s helicopter taking off triggered an air-traffic safety incident at DCA yesterday when Marine One potentially got closer than the acceptable range between aircraft.

A California judge held the Homeland Security Department in contempt for allegedly slow-rolling an order to produce data from last year’s controversial Los Angeles immigration raids.

Trump sought to shield his business finances from the BBC in a defamation lawsuit in an emergency stay motion today.





THE STATES

Amir Hassan, the Trump-endorsed candidate in MI-8, trailed Thomas J. Smith by about 17 percentage points after yesterday’s primary — even though Smith had already dropped out of the race. Smith accepted his nomination in a statement today.

  • Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar lost his reelection bid in MI-13 to state Rep. Donavan McKinney, and conceded the race today.

entries.title: Federal Judge Holds DHS in Contempt Over Immigration Agents’ Text Records
entries.summary: DHS must pay $500 a day until it turns over data from agents’ personal cellphones used in Operation At Large in Los Angeles last year.
entries.content:
A federal judge in California held the Department of Homeland Security in contempt for not complying with an order to search and turn over communications in federal agents’ cellphones about immigration operations in Los Angeles, according to court documents unsealed Tuesday.

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong wrote in her order, filed July 28, that the court had provided the federal government “plenty of time” to find messages kept on agents’ personal phones relating to 15 immigration enforcement actions under Operation At Large last year.

The American Civil Liberties Union, Public Counsel and other immigration advocacy groups requested the material as part of an effort to halt federal immigration agents from using an individual’s perceived race to conduct stops.

“Given that Plaintiffs have shown by clear and convincing evidence that the Defendants

violated a specific and definite order of the court, the burden shifted to Defendants to demonstrate why they were unable to comply,” Frimpong wrote in her contempt order. “They have failed to do so.”

Frimpong ordered DHS to pay $500 every day until it complies with the order to turn over imaging of the phone messages. DHS must also reimburse the lawsuits’ plaintiffs — five Latino workers and other advocacy organizations — for the “time and costs spent by their attorneys in getting the government to comply” with the order.

Body camera footage obtained through court-ordered discovery has revealed federal immigration agents calling Latinos racial slurs during Operation At Large. Text message screenshots filed as exhibits contained conversations of agents exchanging locations of where Latino workers gather, as well as worried talks about possible violations of a temporary restraining order that prohibited indiscriminate arrests.

In December, DHS told the court that agents do not use texting functions on their mobile phones for professional duties, the court order says. Five individuals later testified that month that they, in fact, did use their personal phones for work. DHS argued again in April that agents’ personal phones were outside its possession, custody and control.

A magistrate judge rebutted DHS’ arguments in July and stated that the forensic imaging order remained in effect.

DHS submitted its first payment for violating the court on Tuesday in the amount of $3,500, according to court documents.

entries.title: Commanders to Sign Stefon Diggs, Shoring Up a Shaky Receivers Room
entries.summary: The former Patriot is expected to slot in as Washington’s No. 2 receiver, answering one of the offseason’s biggest questions.
entries.content:
Commanders fans' long nightmare is over. After a spring and summer full of rumors, opinions, guesses and many, many social media posts, Washington got its No. 2 receiver on Wednesday as the team is set to sign veteran free agent Stefon Diggs. The former Patriot has agreed to a one-year, $12 million contract, according to ESPN.

The signing of Diggs, who totaled 85 receptions for 1,013 yards and four touchdowns for the AFC champion Patriots last season, transforms Washington’s receiving corps from an average group to a position of strength.

A source close to Diggs said the 32-year-old DMV native chose Washington because he was impressed by the entire organization, from the front office to the coaches to the players.

Diggs, a four-time Pro Bowler, wanted a “chance to play with one of best young [quarterbacks] and opposite one of [the] best receivers — and to do it all at home,” the source said.

The 2015 fifth-round pick out of Maryland has been one of the most decorated and consistent receivers in the league for nearly a decade. His 9,032 receiving yards since 2018 is the third-most in that time period behind only Davante Adams (9,822) and Tyreek Hill (9,587).

His primary strengths are his route-running and catch radius, skills best highlighted by his famous “Minneapolis Miracle” catch with the Vikings during the 2017 playoffs. According to Next Gen Stats, Diggs had the highest catch percentage (83.3%) in the league last season.

Putting a player with 942 career receptions, 11,504 yards and 74 touchdowns alongside Terry McLaurin (498 receptions, 6,961 yards and 41 touchdowns) makes the receiving unit deep and dangerous. The two veterans will be grouped with promising rookie Antonio Williams, who has had breakout moments during training camp; former first-rounder Treylon Burks; veteran Van Jefferson and a host of other young receivers.

Diggs spent the first five seasons of his career with the Vikings before being traded to the Bills in 2020. After four years in Buffalo, Diggs played in Houston before joining the Patriots and reaching last year’s Super Bowl.

Diggs has also garnered headlines away from the field. In May, he was found not guilty of assaulting his private chef. He is currently suing a social media influencer who has accused him of sexual assault and facing a civil lawsuit for accusing a former concierge of stealing his Ferrari.
