entries.title: Senate Confirms Erica Schwartz to Lead the CDC
entries.summary: Schwartz served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first administration.
entries.content:
Erica Schwartz, who was the deputy U.S. surgeon general during the first Trump administration, will serve as the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The Senate confirmed her nomination Wednesday. When sworn in, Schwartz will be the CDC’s first permanent director in nearly a year, taking over an agency that’s been at the center of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s attempts to transform the nation’s vaccine policies.

The last permanent director, Susan Monarez, was ousted from the role last August after disagreeing with Kennedy on vaccine policies.

National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya has led the CDC in an acting capacity since Monarez’s departure.

The CDC has been rocked by a series of challenges over the past two years, including the measles and hantavirus outbreaks, personnel and funding cuts, and a shooting at its Atlanta campus last summer that killed one police officer.

The agency has also been targeted by the administration with efforts to roll back its vaccine policy, efforts that drew the ire of Sen. Bill Cassidy, who chairs the Senate Committee for Health, Education, Labor and Pensions. Cassidy ultimately said he would support Schwartz after the CDC updated a website about vaccines and autism to remove a reference to him.

Schwartz, the former chief medical officer of the Coast Guard, told Cassidy during her confirmation hearing that she would “never betray the science.”

entries.title: Max Miller’s Corporate Backers Go Silent on Embattled Congressman
entries.summary: Dozens of company and trade group PACs refuse to say whether they’ll ditch — or defend — the Ohio Republican.
entries.content:
Dozens of different corporate interests combined to fill Rep. Max Miller’s reelection account with six-figures worth of campaign cash in recent weeks.

But now, amid accusations that Miller abused his daughter and now ex-wife — accusations the congressman denies — his business allies are falling silent.

Of the more than 35 corporate and trade association political action committees that contributed at least $1,000 to Miller’s campaign since mid-April, according to Federal Election Commission records, all either ignored or declined to answer questions from NOTUS about their relationship with the Republican lawmaker.

Among those questions: Do they continue to support Miller for a third term representing Ohio’s 7th Congressional District? Have they requested refunds of previous donations? Will they give Miller’s campaign money in the future?

Among the corporate PACs that wouldn’t openly distance themselves from — or defend — Miller: TD Bank, Citigroup, ConocoPhillips, John Deere & Co., Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, Pfizer, Genentech, Cencora, Altria, Tenaska and Elevance Health.

Trade association PACs that are remaining similarly mum on Miller include those of the Allied Pilots Association, Advanced Medical Technology Association, America’s Health Insurance Plans, American Dental Association, American Academy of Sleep Medicine, American Investment Council, American Bankers Association, International Franchise Association, International Council of Shopping Centers, Investment Company Institute, National Apartment Association, National Roofing Contractors Association, National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors, Healthcare Distribution Alliance, National Association of Convenience Stores, National Electrical Contractors Association, Ohio Corn and Wheat Growers Association, United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America and the Farm Credit Council.

Associated General Contractors of America spokesperson Brian Turmail confirmed in an email that his organization’s PAC contributed $2,500 to Miller’s campaign this spring, but he wouldn’t otherwise comment.

Meanwhile, several special interest group PACs also did not respond to repeated inquiries, including the House Conservatives Fund, American Israel Public Affairs Committee and Pakistani American Public Affairs Committee.

Miller’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment on whether PACs have requested refunds or otherwise communicated their future intentions.

Miller says he isn’t dropping out of his race despite the accusations and a call for him to step aside by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), the father of Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno.

“If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” Bernie Moreno wrote on X. “I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.”

This week, Miller’s attorney released naked photos of Miller’s young daughter and also revealed her name as part of a cache of documents intended to bolster Miller’s assertions of innocence. The attorney, Aaron Minc, said the release was “completely unintentional and a mistake.”

Miller, for his part, told PBS News Hour: “No criminal charge has ever been filed against me. My former wife is engaging in a pattern of reporting incredible, serious and destructive allegations with absolutely no evidence.”

Ohio law gives Republicans a deadline of Monday to replace a congressional nominee on the November ballot, meaning Miller would have to abandon his reelection campaign by then in order for the party to nominate someone else.

As matters stand, Miller is set to face Democrat Brian Poindexter in a race the Cook Political Report scores as “likely Republican.”

entries.title: Republicans Roll the Dice on Their Farm Bill
entries.summary: With time running out, senators plow forward with their compromise, hoping Democrats come along.
entries.content:
The Senate Agriculture Committee will take up its version of the farm bill Thursday, with provisions meant to help farmers with financial aid, crop sales overseas and year-round sales of ethanol-blend gasoline.

But the outcome is unclear, particularly without a clear bipartisan deal on parts of the measure dealing with when some states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

The current short-term extension of the farm bill expires at the end of September. Chair John Boozman (R-Arkansas), after weeks of negotiations, released a compromise bill text and emphasized the need to act ahead of the August recess.

“We need to act this week, or we run out of time,” Boozman said.

Farm bankruptcies are at record highs largely due to several consecutive years of high input prices and extreme weather. The Senate bill attempts to help farmers on both fronts, by giving farmers more flexibility to use emergency government land and cost-sharing programs during droughts and floods.

The bill also changes how conservation payments are calculated so farmers with drought- or flood-prone land receive more support. And it raises the size of loans farmers can access, puts more money into helping U.S. crops sell overseas and expands support for newer farming technology that helps producers use less fertilizer and fuel per acre.

The most contentious piece remains how to handle SNAP payment error rates. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), who farms corn and soybeans with his family and has been in the Senate since 1980, said this has been the most difficult farm bill to get bipartisan support for in his career.

“I think every other farm bill that I’ve worked on in the 46 years I've been in the United States Senate has been a bipartisan bill,” Grassley told reporters. “It seems like this year, it’s very difficult to get Democratic support, mostly over a food stamp issue.”

Democrats have asked for a two-year delay in the cost shift to states with SNAP payment error rates above 6%, which is scheduled to start next year. Republicans have preferred to leave the changes made to SNAP in a 2025 reconciliation law.

Boozman’s bill met Democrats halfway, with a one-year delay. In exchange, states with higher error rates would pay a bigger share of the cost than in the original reforms passed in the reconciliation law.

Boozman has acknowledged that many states simply need more time. Only nine states and the Virgin Islands have error rates belowthe 6% threshold, according to data gathered by the USDA.

Democrats aren’t sold. Ranking member Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota) hasn’t made her thoughts on the updated text public. Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) is encouraging Democrats to hold out for a better deal.

“Democrats should remain united and only support a Farm Bill that includes a clean two-year delay of the SNAP cost shift to states,” Booker said in a statement.

One compromise included is the bill is language authorizing permanent, nationwide year-round sales of E15, the 15%-ethanol blend corn growers have chased for years.

But the provision has garnered the ire of oil producers and their representatives. A provision to approve year-round E15 in the House version of the farm bill nearly derailed the bill’s progress on the House floor, but ended up passing in a separate vote in May.

Complicating all of it is the absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky). Republicans and Democrats effectively enter Thursday’s markup with even numbers, raising the odds that Boozman will need Democratic votes just to move the bill out of committee.
